qualifiers.population: adults and children aged 10 years and older

triples.evidence_text: Metformin is a first-line treatment used for type 2 diabetes in adults and children 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar levels. It is also used off-label to improve symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and other conditions. Metformin tablets should be used together with dietary changes and exercise for better results.

Metformin is a first-line treatment used for type 2 diabetes in adults and children 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar levels. It is also used off-label to improve symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) and other conditions. Metformin tablets should be used together with dietary changes and exercise for better results.
Metformin belongs to the drug class biguanides.

Metformin works by reducing glucose absorption from the intestines, lowering liver glucose production, and improving insulin sensitivity. Managing blood sugar levels with medications like metformin can prevent diabetes complications such as kidney damage, nerve issues, blindness, amputations, sexual dysfunction, and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Metformin has a boxed warning for lactic acidosis, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid in your blood, which can cause death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. A boxed warning is the strongest safety-related warning issued by the FDA.
Vitamin B12 deficiency: Metformin can lower your vitamin B12 levels over time. Your doctor may check your blood counts every year and your B12 levels every 2 to 3 years to catch any problems early.

triples.entity_1: Metformin combined with insulin or insulin-release-promoting diabetes medicines
triples.evidence_text: Low blood sugar when taken with insulin or other diabetes medicines: Taking metformin along with insulin or certain other diabetes drugs (ones that boost insulin release) raises the risk of low blood sugar. If you're on one of these combinations, your doctor may lower the dose of the other medicine.

Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients. In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.

You should not use metformin if you have:

Metformin immediate release tablets should not be given to a child younger than 10 years old.
This medicine should not be used for type 1 diabetes.

Talk to your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. Metformin can pass into your breast milk. Your healthcare provider will be able to advise you about the best way to feed your baby while you take this medicine.
Take metformin with a meal, unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Some forms of metformin are taken only once daily with the evening meal. Follow your doctor's instructions.

triples.entity_2: 500 mg orally twice a day or 850 mg orally once a day
triples.evidence_text:
Usual Adult Metformin Dose for Diabetes Type 2:
Immediate-release tablets:
Initial dose: 500 mg orally twice a day or 850 mg orally once a day Dose titration: Increase by 500 mg increments weekly or 850 mg every 2 weeks as tolerated. Maintenance dose: 2000 mg/day in divided doses Maximum dose: 2550 mg/day. Doses above 2,000 mg may be better tolerated given 3 times

triples.entity_1: Topiramate, zonisamide, acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide combined with metformin
triples.section_title: What other drugs will affect metformin?
triples.evidence_text: Medicines that have a carbonic anhydrase inhibiting effect like topiramate (often used for seizures or migraines), zonisamide (used for seizures), acetazolamide (used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and other conditions), and dichlorphenamide (used for a muscle condition called periodic paralysis) can raise the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis when taken with metformin. These medicines commonly lower a substance in your blood called bicarbonate, which your body needs to keep its acid levels balanced. If you're taking metformin along with any of these medicines, your doctor may want to monitor you more closely.

triples.section_title: What other drugs will affect metformin?
triples.evidence_text: Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.

triples.section_title: What other drugs will affect metformin?
triples.evidence_text: Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.
